title: HDD write precompensation applied to bitline-coupling-aware cell restore
idea: Hard disks shift write timing according to neighbouring bits to cancel intersymbol interference. The DRAM write driver/sense amp reads the neighbouring bitlines' data already latched in the row buffer and gives an extra restore boost (slightly higher or longer restore) only to cells whose neighbour pattern (e.g. 0-1-0) is worst case for coupling noise at the next sense.
why: Bitline-to-bitline coupling eats roughly 20-30% of sense margin at 4.5-5 fF (fact 1). Getting that margin back lets the capacitor shrink 15-25%, or lets refresh run about 1.5x longer.

title: Shingled DRAM bands with built-in neighbour restore, like SMR drives
idea: Shingled magnetic recording overlaps tracks and accepts that a write must rewrite its neighbours. In the same way, rows are packed at a pitch that is deliberately weak to hammer and grouped into bands of 8-16. Each ACT also schedules a hidden pipelined restore of rows i+-1 in a parallel subarray slot, so the protection is built into the structure and does not depend on counters.
why: Designing for a hammer threshold of ~100 instead of ~1k (fact 9) frees about 10% of wordline pitch, giving a 10-15% density gain. The mitigation tables go away. The cost is extra restore energy on each ACT.

title: Battery-management Kalman estimator of per-region cell charge
idea: A BMS estimates a battery's state of charge with a Kalman filter. The memory controller runs a lightweight filter per region. Its inputs are temperature telemetry, the access history (every access restores charge) and occasional sentinel-read measurements. Refresh is issued only when the lower confidence bound of the estimated charge approaches the sense threshold.
why: Refresh costs ~46 fJ/bit and 16-33% of idle power (fact 3). Model-based refresh with a bounded error probability could cut it by 50-75%.

title: Battery reconditioning pulses that reset variable-retention-time traps
idea: Deep-cycle reconditioning breaks up sulfate crystals in lead-acid batteries. During idle, each row would get a brief reconditioning pulse: a deep negative wordline plus a raised bitline/substrate bias. The pulse empties the metastable gate- and junction-region traps that flip cells into their leaky VRT state. The pulsed rows are then re-profiled.
why: VRT is why per-cell retention profiling cannot be trusted, and therefore why 64 ms worst-case refresh is still needed (fact 3). Collapsing the VRT tail would make profile-based refresh safe, cutting refresh 2-4x.

title: OLED-demura-style e-beam charge-decay imaging of leaky junctions inline
idea: OLED fabs photograph every panel to build a per-pixel compensation map. Before the capacitor is built, the storage-node contacts would be flood-charged with an e-beam and voltage-contrast imaged twice, seconds apart. Contacts that lose contrast quickly mark leaky junction outliers across the wafer in parallel. Those coordinates feed process learning and are written into die fuse maps.
why: This attacks the leakage tail (fact 3) at its source, and the faster yield learning cuts retention-test cost. It could catch the worst ~0.01% of cells before the capacitor modules are spent on them.

title: OLED burn-in ledger that trims subarray wordline voltages over life
idea: OLED drivers count the cumulative on-time of each pixel and boost the aged pixels. The DRAM would accumulate the activation-time integral of each subarray in a small counter. Local regulators then trim that subarray's VPP and negative-wordline level to track the access-transistor Vth drift from BTI/HCI, so the full end-of-life guardband is not applied from day one.
why: This recovers ~100-200 mV of lifetime guardband against the voltage floor (fact 10): about 10-15% wordline energy, or a tighter leakage tail early in life.

title: LCD polarity inversion: per-row epoch flip of stored data
idea: LCDs invert pixel polarity every frame so that DC stress does not cause image sticking. Each row stores its data XORed with a per-row epoch bit that toggles on every scrub pass, so no cell or access transistor holds the same charge polarity for months. The controller decodes with the flag bit.
why: This balances BTI and data-pattern-dependent charge trapping, which drive aging and VRT, and it defeats hammer patterns tuned to particular data. It could shrink aging guardbands and data-dependent retention outliers by an estimated ~2x.

title: Synonymous-codon encoding that hides known weak cells
idea: Synonymous codons let DNA tolerate mutations without changing the protein. Each 8-bit symbol is written into 9 cells. Using the row's known weak-cell map, and the fact that a true cell leaks only 1->0, the encoder picks the synonymous codeword that places a discharged '0' in every known leaky cell (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memory with defects). Weak cells then never hold charge that can leak.
why: With ~12% overhead, cells with poor retention (fact 3) stay in service and refresh is no longer set by the tail. Refresh could stretch 4-8x for rows with mapped defects.

title: Reinsurance pool: rack-level CXL spare memory absorbing failing pages
idea: Reinsurers pool rare risks across many insurers. Each rack keeps a shared CXL-attached spare pool of about 2% of rack capacity. The hypervisor live-migrates pages from any DIMM whose correctable-error rate rises into the pool, so individual DIMMs ship with thinner margins and fewer on-die spare rows.
why: Pooled spares scale with sqrt(N) instead of N. That recovers ~3-5% of die area spent on redundancy and raises yield, so cost per bit falls.

title: Spot-market auction allocating weak rows to error-tolerant buyers
idea: Markets price goods of different quality. The OS sorts profiled rows into reliability grades and runs an internal auction. Each process declares how much error it tolerates: kernel structures none, video frames, KV-cache and activations some. Weak rows that would otherwise be retired or refreshed 4x go to the tolerant bidders at relaxed refresh.
why: The retention tail stops setting the global refresh rate (fact 3) and becomes a priced resource. Refresh could fall 20-40%, and the ~1-3% of weak cells stay usable.

title: Seismic base isolation: grounded shield rail buried between wordlines
idea: Base isolation decouples a building from ground shaking. A thin grounded TiN or doped-poly rail is buried in the isolation trench between adjacent buried wordlines. It terminates the fringing fields and collects the electrons injected by the aggressor before they reach the victim storage-node junctions.
why: It could raise the row-hammer threshold about 10x, from ~1k to ~10k ACTs (fact 9), removing most counter area and RFM bandwidth. The cost is a small increase in pitch.

title: Seismograph sensor measuring actual substrate disturbance, not activation counts
idea: Seismographs measure real ground motion rather than predicting it. Each subarray gets a well-tap sense resistor and an integrator that measures the minority-carrier/substrate charge actually injected by wordline toggling and long row-open times. When the integrated charge near a region passes a calibrated fraction of Cs*dV, targeted refresh fires.
why: Mitigation then responds to physics instead of a counter proxy, so it catches RowPress and many-sided patterns (fact 9). Refresh spent on false alarms could fall about 50%.

title: Adaptive-optics guide-star canary cells in every subarray
idea: Adaptive optics measures the atmosphere with a bright guide star. Each subarray holds about 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (smaller cap, closer spacing) that fail at ~1/2 the retention time and ~1/2 the hammer count of normal cells. A comparator scan during refresh catches canary flips and locally doubles refresh or restores the neighbours.
why: Nominal refresh can then be set for typical conditions while canaries give in-situ early warning. That cuts refresh 40-60% (fact 3) and adds a hammer tripwire (fact 9).

title: OFDM pilot cells that calibrate each row's sense reference
idea: OFDM inserts known pilot tones to estimate the channel. Each row stores a few pilot cells holding known 1s and 0s, rewritten at every restore. At sense time the pilots' developed bitline voltages set a row-specific sense reference. The reference therefore tracks how far that row has decayed since its last restore, and its temperature.
why: This recovers ~30% of sense margin, so Cs can drop toward ~3.5 fF (fact 1) or refresh can run 2x longer (fact 3).

title: HDR exposure bracketing: double sensing that flags erasures
idea: HDR photography brackets exposures to capture the marginal tones. A replica latch senses each line again with +delta and -delta reference offsets. Bits whose answers disagree are flagged as erasures, and the on-die RS/BCH decoder runs erasure decoding, which corrects about twice as many flagged symbols as unknown errors with the same parity.
why: Effective ECC strength roughly doubles, so the raw weak-cell rate can be 10-100x higher. That allows smaller capacitors or longer refresh (facts 1 and 3).

title: MEMS-style post-package trimming of sense-amplifier offsets
idea: MEMS gyros and oscillators are trimmed after packaging to cancel fabrication asymmetry. Each sense-amp pair gets a 3-bit capacitor-DAC trim. Final test sweeps it, and the codes go into a compact on-die OTP array, removing the systematic offset that sets worst-case signal margin.
why: Cutting SA offset sigma from ~15-25 mV to ~5 mV lets the cell signal fall ~30%: a smaller Cs (fact 1) or a weaker transistor. The trim area is small next to periphery at ~49% of the die (fact 7).

title: Fiber-Bragg distributed thermometry setting per-mat refresh rates
idea: Fiber Bragg gratings measure temperature every metre along a fiber. Tiny diode or ring-oscillator thermometers are placed in every mat, and each mat's refresh multiplier follows its own temperature: hot spots under an HBM base die or next to a GPU get 2x, cool mats get 1x. Today the whole die refreshes at its worst-case temperature.
why: Retention halves for every ~10 C, and HBM stacks carry 10-20 C gradients. Matching refresh to each mat's temperature cuts refresh 30-50% (facts 3 and 6).

title: Chocolate-tempering anneal cycles for capacitor dielectric phase purity
idea: Chocolatiers cycle temperature so that only the stable Form V crystals survive. The ZrO2/HfO2 capacitor dielectric would get a cycled RTP profile: above the phase transition, cooled to nucleate, then reheated just below the melt point of the unstable phases. This dissolves the minority monoclinic and amorphous pockets and the vacancy-rich grain boundaries that make up the leakage tail.
why: A narrower leakage distribution could mean ~10x fewer weak cells and possibly k toward 45-50. Both relax the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the retention tail.

title: Water-hammer arrestor: transient deep-negative clamp on neighbour wordlines
idea: Plumbing arrestors absorb pressure spikes. While wordline i rises and falls, the sub-wordline drivers of i+-1 and i+-2 pulse deeper negative (about -0.5 V instead of -0.2 V), but only for the edge window. That damps capacitive coupling and electron injection into victims without the GIDL penalty that a constant deep negative bias would carry.
why: Could raise the hammer threshold 3-10x (fact 9) without counters, using only sub-wordline driver timing.

title: Sail-reefing mode: elastic conversion to twin-cell under thermal stress
idea: Sailors reef sails when the wind is high. When die temperature exceeds 85 C or the error rate climbs, the OS can switch selected subarrays from 1T1C to 2T2C twin-cell mode: complementary data in paired cells with differential sensing. That halves capacity but doubles the signal and stretches retention about 4x. Memory hot-unplug absorbs the lost capacity.
why: This avoids the 2x refresh penalty at high temperature (fact 3) and lets nominal cells be built weaker, because they have a safe fallback mode.

title: Apoptotic rows: autonomous self-test and soft repair during self-refresh
idea: Cells that detect their own damage trigger programmed death (apoptosis). During self-refresh, an on-die BIST samples rows at extended retention. Rows that fail retire themselves and swap in spare rows through soft-PPR registers, which persist in a small OTP block. The die reports the swaps to the host through mode registers.
why: The die heals VRT and aging failures in the field without host ECC escalation. Factory retention test time can shrink (test cost), and fewer DUEs reach the host.

title: Grid protective relays isolating shorted mats at runtime
idea: Power grids open relays to isolate faulted segments and keep the rest live. Each mat's VPP/VBLP feed gets a tiny current monitor and pass gate. A wordline-bitline or capacitor short drawing excess current trips isolation for that mat alone, and its addresses remap to a spare mat. Today such a short kills the bank or the die.
why: Shorts are a top yield killer on large dies, so this could add ~3-8% yield. It also makes the die resilient to hard shorts that appear in the field.

title: Tuned-mass-damper resonance detector: spectral hammer detection without counters
idea: A tuned mass damper targets one resonant frequency of a building. Hammering is periodic, so each bank runs a few Goertzel/autocorrelation bins over a hashed row-address stream. Aggressor sequences that recur at a fixed lag, including many-sided TRRespass patterns, stand out using about 10-20 registers. The detected aggressors get neighbour refresh.
why: Tracking SRAM could shrink ~90% compared with per-row counters (PRAC) while catching patterns that sampling TRR misses (facts 7 and 9).

title: Bain-marie phase-change heat buffer clipping DIMM temperature spikes
idea: A bain-marie holds food below 100 C. A paraffin or salt-hydrate PCM pouch melting at ~78-80 C is bonded into the DIMM heatspreader. During load bursts it absorbs latent heat and holds the dies below 85 C, so the 2x refresh rule never triggers. Off-the-shelf PCM, a thermal chamber and qualification fit in under 12 months and under $300k.
why: Avoiding 2x refresh in hot servers saves ~10% bandwidth and 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and it keeps the retention tail in its nominal regime.

title: Flight-recorder DIMM interposer capturing command history before each error
idea: An aircraft's black box records the minutes before an incident. An FPGA DIMM interposer (two board spins, about $250k) keeps a rolling 1-second ring buffer of ACT/REF commands and temperature. On any corrected or uncorrected ECC event it freezes and dumps the buffer. Deployed on ~200 partner servers within the $1M, it would build the first large dataset linking real flips to real access patterns.
why: Measured distributions of hammer and retention tails, rather than worst-case assumptions, allow right-sized mitigation and refresh margins, possibly a 2x relaxation (facts 3 and 9).

title: Bridge load-posting: measured per-module hammer limits written to SPD
idea: Bridges post weight limits from inspection rather than from design worst case. An open FPGA tester for commodity DDR5 (5 rigs at about $50k each) measures each module's minimum hammer threshold and retention tail in about 20 minutes and writes them to SPD vendor bytes. A BIOS patch then sets RFM/PRAC thresholds and refresh per module.
why: Most modules are far stronger than the worst case. Per-module settings cut mitigation bandwidth and refresh 30-60% (facts 3 and 9) with no new silicon.

title: Actuarially insured B-grade DRAM on FPGA-CXL cards
idea: Outlets sell factory 'seconds' with a warranty attached. Buy retention-rejected or down-binned dies and modules (fail at 64 ms, pass at 32 ms; sold 10-30% cheaper or scrapped). Mount them behind an FPGA CXL controller that refreshes at 2x and applies strong symbol ECC, and price the warranty from logged error data. Pilot 1,000 cards within the $1M budget.
why: Turns a scrap stream into usable capacity during the 4x shortage, at an estimated 30-50% lower cost per bit and no new wafer capital (fact 4).

title: Urban-mining refurbishment line for retired server DIMMs
idea: Urban mining pulls metals out of e-waste; this recovers the bits instead. A semi-automated line tests decommissioned DDR4 from retired fleets, maps weak rows, rewrites SPD, and deploys the modules behind FPGA CXL-DDR4 adapters that hide the weak-row map through page retirement. Test racks, adapters and 3 staff fit within $1M.
why: Millions of retired DIMMs a year become supply at near-zero fab capital (fact 4), and recycling also works around the resource chokepoints.

title: Solar MPPT perturb-and-observe tuning of per-bank refresh
idea: Solar inverters wiggle their operating point to track maximum power. Firmware in an open FPGA/CXL controller periodically lengthens one bank's refresh interval by a step and watches patrol-scrub correctable-error counts for a window. It keeps the step while errors stay flat and backs off when they rise, so it tracks each bank's true minimum refresh as temperature and aging drift.
why: Cuts refresh energy and bandwidth 40-70% (fact 3) using only controller firmware, which fits a 24-month, $1M scope.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes matched to true-cell and anti-cell leakage
idea: Optical on-off links lose photons but never create them (the Z-channel). DRAM retention errors are one-way per cell type: true cells go 1->0, anti-cells 0->1. A quick test maps each part's true/anti layout. The FPGA controller then uses asymmetric-error-correcting codes (Varshamov/constant-weight style) that correct t one-way errors with about half the parity symmetric BCH needs.
why: The same parity budget corrects ~2x the retention errors, so refresh intervals can stretch 2-4x (fact 3). It is pure coding plus firmware, which fits the budget.

title: Context decoding: data-type priors resolve uncorrectable memory errors
idea: Readers fix typos from context. On a detected-uncorrectable error, the kernel lists the candidate codewords at minimum distance that fit the syndrome. It picks the one plausible for the data type: a pointer that is aligned and inside a valid VA range, a float exponent within the tensor's range, valid UTF-8, legal page-table bits. Type tags come from the compiler or the allocator, and the Linux patch plus evaluation fit within $1M.
why: Turning ~50-80% of DUEs into corrections allows cheaper ECC or relaxed refresh on weaker DRAM (facts 3 and 8).

title: Fishing zones and quotas: tenant-exclusive subarrays with boundary ACT limits
idea: Fisheries combine exclusive economic zones with catch quotas instead of tracking each fish. The FPGA/CXL controller gives each tenant (VM/ASID) exclusive subarray zones, so hammering inside a zone harms only its owner. Only boundary rows, about 1-2% of all rows, carry small ACT counters with strict quotas.
why: Cross-tenant hammer protection with ~50x less tracking SRAM, and it scales to thresholds of ~100 (fact 9). It needs only controller logic and kernel allocation.

title: Anti-lock-brake pulsed row-open time cap against RowPress
idea: ABS pulses the brakes so the wheels never lock. The open-source FPGA controller caps continuous row-open time (tAggON) at ~200 ns. A row being held open for hits has its buffer copied to a controller-side row cache and is closed early. That defeats RowPress, which multiplies flips 10-100x when rows stay open long.
why: Keeps ACT-count-based protection valid without 10x over-provisioning mitigation (fact 9). It is a policy change demonstrable on DDR5 within budget.

title: Noise-shaped bit-plane placement of AI tensors in weak rows
idea: Audio noise shaping pushes quantization noise into bands nobody hears. Weights and KV-cache are stored bit-plane transposed. Sign, exponent and high mantissa planes go to profiled strong rows with ECC. Low mantissa planes go to weak rows at relaxed refresh (about 1 s) with no ECC, where any flips land as tiny numeric noise. The software allocator and profiler fit within $1M.
why: Refresh on 50-70% of AI memory could drop 10x, the ECC overhead goes away for those planes, and accuracy loss stays below ~0.1% (facts 3 and 5).

title: Holographic spreading: Walsh-Hadamard encoding of tolerant data before storage
idea: Every fragment of a hologram holds a blurred copy of the whole image. The accelerator or controller applies a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to each 64-value block before writing and clips on the inverse. A flipped bit then becomes small noise spread over 64 values instead of one catastrophic exponent error. It runs on existing hardware in firmware or kernels.
why: Error-tolerant data (activations, images) degrade gracefully in weak or rarely refreshed memory, giving refresh and ECC savings on 30-60% of AI capacity (fact 3).

title: Minimum-equipment-list grading: ship partial-good dies with signed fault maps
idea: Airliners dispatch legally with documented inoperative equipment. Draft a JEDEC-style SPD extension that carries a signed fault map (dead mats, weak rows). Write reference BIOS and CXL firmware that route around the mapped faults, and pilot 100 modules built from partial-good dies that are scrapped today. All of it fits in $1M.
why: Effective die yield up 5-15% at advanced nodes means more sellable bits per wafer and lower capital per bit (fact 4).

title: Andon-cord fleet telemetry loop from datacenters back to fab test
idea: At Toyota, any worker can pull the andon cord and push a root cause upstream. A neutral consortium collects anonymized per-die correctable-error signatures from hyperscaler fleets, keyed by die ID, and correlates them with wafer, lot and die position. It reports back to the fabs which test screens can relax and which must tighten. Data platform plus two pilots fit in $1M.
why: Test time down 20-30%, fewer good dies binned down, and fewer field DUEs. It also gives a U.S. entrant a feedback channel it could not otherwise get.

title: Companion planting: pair hammer-heavy pages with self-healing neighbours
idea: Gardeners plant companions that protect each other. A kernel page allocator uses the reverse-engineered DRAM address map to put physically adjacent rows next to frequently activated pages. Those adjacent rows are filled with data that rewrites itself every few ms anyway (ring buffers, network and DMA rings, scratch), or with guard and free pages. Hammer victims therefore heal on their own.
why: Raises the effective hammer tolerance with no hardware change (fact 9), as a pure kernel patch within budget.

title: CD-style cross-interleaved two-level code across banks
idea: CDs survive 2.5 mm scratches with CIRC: two Reed-Solomon codes plus delay interleaving. In the FPGA controller, an inner RS code per 64 B burst detects and flags errors. An outer RS code spans 28 lines that address-mapping skew places in different banks and subarrays. A hammered row or dead wordline, the 'scratch', then corrupts at most one symbol per outer codeword.
why: Survives whole-row and wordline failures at ~12% overhead, so chips can ship with fewer row spares and weaker hammer margins (fact 9).

title: Fractional-reserve parity: one XOR row backs many detection-only rows
idea: Banks hold reserves for only a fraction of deposits because withdrawals are rare. Each line keeps only a detection CRC-8. One XOR parity row in another bank backs each group of 32 rows. On a detected error, the line is rebuilt from the other 31 plus parity on a slow path. A controller write cache coalesces the parity read-modify-writes.
why: ECC storage overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3-6% while still correcting whole-line errors (cost per bit). It can be implemented in FPGA controller logic.

title: Epidemic contact tracing: ECC events trigger blast-radius refresh
idea: Epidemiologists trace and test the contacts of each case. When row r reports a corrected error, controller firmware treats it as a case. It immediately refreshes and scrubs r+-1..+-4 using the physical adjacency map. If more cases appear, it raises local refresh and asks the OS to quarantine (remap) the hot aggressor pages.
why: Free ECC events become hammer and weak-cell sensors (facts 3 and 9), and stop cascades before they reach uncorrectable errors. It needs firmware and a kernel hook only.

title: Pharma accelerated-stability Arrhenius screening to shorten retention test
idea: Pharma predicts two-year shelf life from short accelerated aging. Short retention tests at three elevated temperatures, combined with Bayesian extrapolation of each die's retention tail and VRT probability, replace long nominal-temperature retention loops. The method is validated on 10k dies with a partner test house.
why: Test time and cost down 30-50%, and fewer false rejects raise yield. It is a methods and statistics project well within $1M.

title: Frequency-hopping row remap with rotating secret keys
idea: Spread-spectrum radios hop channels on a secret sequence to defeat jammers. The FPGA controller applies a keyed small-Feistel permutation from logical to physical rows within each bank. It re-keys gradually, one row-pair swap per refresh interval, so an attacker never learns adjacency and aggressor ACTs spread over many victims.
why: Removes targeted hammering and raises the effective threshold about 10x (fact 9) with controller logic only.

title: HARQ incremental redundancy: strong parity fetched only on decode failure
idea: LTE's HARQ sends extra redundancy only when the first decode fails. Light SEC-DED is stored inline, and strong BCH/RS incremental parity lives in a separate parity region in another bank. The controller fetches the strong parity only when the inline decode flags an uncorrectable error. Writes to the parity region are coalesced.
why: Strong correction (tolerating 10-100x more weak cells, so refresh can run 2-4x longer) at near-zero read-bandwidth cost (facts 3 and 5). FPGA demo on DDR5.

title: Safety-stock ECC: spare parity chips loaned as capacity while healthy
idea: Inventory systems size safety stock to demand variance. On 10-chip DDR5 ECC DIMMs, the FPGA/CXL controller packs data into the two ECC chips for regions with a measured-low error rate, protecting them with a small CRC carved from the data. When telemetry shows errors rising, the region converts back to full ECC and the OS gives the capacity back.
why: Adds up to +25% usable capacity from existing DIMMs in healthy regions during the shortage, while weak regions keep full protection.

title: Diversified-portfolio DIMMs mixing vendors inside each codeword
idea: Portfolio theory cuts risk by holding uncorrelated assets. Build ECC modules in which the chips of each codeword come from 2-3 vendors or process lots. Systematic weaknesses (TRR bypass patterns, temperature-dependent retention) then stay uncorrelated, and chipkill absorbs one vendor's failure mode. Module design, qualification and a pilot run fit in $1M.
why: Makes cheaper second-source dies, including new or U.S. entrants, usable at low risk. That diversifies supply and lowers cost per bit.
